title: Determinants, Cofactors, and the Inverse: Visual Guide
outline: Title: Determinants, Cofactors, and the Inverse: Visual Guide

1. Pivots Become Volume | the unit square and the parallelogram spanned by the columns of A = [[3, b], [1, d]], with sliders for column 2 and one-tap jumps to independent, dependent and reversed-orientation cases, reading out det, area factor, orientation, rank and invertibility together | the pivot count from RREF and the determinant are the same verdict, and det = 0 is the geometric statement that dependent columns enclose zero area, which is exactly why a singular matrix has no inverse

2. Crossing Out A Minor | a tappable 2x2, 3x3 or 4x4 matrix in which the chosen entry's whole row and column are struck out and the determinant of the surviving block is computed | the indices of M(i,j) name what you delete and never what you keep, and an n x n matrix always leaves an (n-1) x (n-1) block, so a 4x4 gives 3x3 minors

3. The Checkerboard Signs | a 3x3, 4x4 or 5x5 board of + and - signs, with the i + j arithmetic for the square you tap and, on the 3x3, the real minor and cofactor from A = [[2, 1, 0], [3, 4, 5], [0, 1, 1]] | the sign is (-1) to the power i + j, fixed by position alone and never by the entry's value, so minor and cofactor agree on the plus squares and differ by a sign on every minus square

4. Pick Your Expansion Line | three matrices and all six of their rows and columns, each labelled with the number of minors it costs, expanded term by term with the zero entries killed before any minor is computed | every row and every column returns the same determinant, so the only thing your choice changes is the work, and expanding a triangular matrix repeatedly leaves the product of its diagonal

5. Build The Adjugate | A, its cofactor matrix, that matrix transposed, and the product A x adj(A), all recomputed live as the middle entry slides through the value that makes A singular | adj(A) is the cofactor matrix transposed, so the (2,3) slot holds C(3,2); A adj(A) = det(A) I holds for every square matrix including singular ones, and taking determinants gives det(adj A) = det(A) to the power n - 1

6. Two Roads, One Inverse | the adjugate formula, the full Gauss-Jordan trace on the block [A | I], and an undo-a-vector demonstration, with a slider that drives det(A) to 0 | both roads produce the same inverse entry for entry and both break at det(A) = 0 for one shared reason, because a collapsed transformation sends two different inputs to the same output and no matrix can send that output back to both
